entities.summary:
Eugène François Auguste d'Arnauld, baron de Vitrolles (1774-1854) was a French aristocrat and politician.

Born into the nobility of France, d'Arnauld's family played a significant role in the French Revolution.

In 1806, he married Princess Sophie de Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach, and together they had five children.

D'Arnauld was a member of the Chambre des députés and served as a representative for the department of the Loire.

He was also a strong advocate for the abolition of slavery, a cause close to his heart.

D'Arnauld's legacy as a politician and abolitionist continues to be felt in France and beyond.

His remarkable life was marked by both personal and political triumphs, and his commitment to the abolition of slavery remains a powerful testament to his character.

The inscription on his tombstone, 'Sacre de la liberté' ('Sacred to Liberty'), serves as a poignant reminder of his unwavering dedication to this cause.

entities.summary:
Eugène François Auguste d'Arnauld, baron de Vitrolles (1774-1854), was a French aristocrat and politician who played a crucial role in the development of the French monarchy during the early 19th century. As a member of the House of Bourbon, he served as a deputy to the French National Assembly and was a key figure in the Bourbon Restoration of 1815.

D'Arnauld's involvement in politics was marked by his efforts to promote the interests of the French nobility and the Catholic Church. He was a strong supporter of the Bourbon dynasty and worked tirelessly to restore the monarchy to power after the fall of Napoleon Bonaparte.

Despite his efforts, d'Arnauld's legacy is often overshadowed by that of his contemporaries, and he is largely forgotten in modern historical accounts. However, his contributions to the French political landscape of the early 19th century are undeniable, and his role in shaping the course of European history cannot be understated.

As a testament to his enduring legacy, d'Arnauld's name continues to be invoked by historians and scholars today, who recognize the significance of his actions in shaping the modern European state.
